mcqs.question: Why must a service worker be served over HTTPS (or localhost)?
options: HTTPS is required for any JavaScript file larger than 4KB
A network-intercepting script is powerful enough that allowing it over plain HTTP would let a network attacker inject one
Service workers require TLS specifically to access the Cache API
HTTP connections can't support background threads in the browser
mcqs.explanation: A service worker can intercept and rewrite every request in its scope, so serving it over plain HTTP would let a man-in-the-middle attacker on an insecure network inject a malicious worker. File size and thread support have nothing to do with the requirement.

mcqs.question: A new service worker finishes installing while an older version is still controlling open tabs. What happens by default?
options: The new worker enters a waiting state and won't activate until no page is controlled by the old worker
The new worker immediately takes over all tabs, terminating the old one
The new worker's install is rolled back and discarded
Both workers run simultaneously, splitting requests between them
mcqs.explanation: The lifecycle deliberately holds a new worker in waiting to avoid two versions of the app running at once across different tabs — it only activates once every page using the old worker has closed, unless skipWaiting() forces it.

mcqs.question: Which caching strategy serves a cached response immediately while fetching an update in the background for the next request?
options: Cache-first
Network-first
Stale-while-revalidate
Cache-only
mcqs.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate specifically returns the cached copy right away and updates the cache asynchronously in the background, so the user gets instant response now and fresher data on the next request. Cache-first never re-fetches unless the cache misses; network-first waits on the network first.

mcqs.question: A service worker's fetch handler calls fetch(request) to reach the network. Does this bypass the browser's normal HTTP cache?
options: Yes — fetch calls inside a service worker always go straight to the network, ignoring Cache-Control headers
No — that fetch call still goes through the normal HTTP caching rules; the Cache API is a separate store your code manages explicitly on top of it
Yes, but only if the service worker has an existing Cache API entry for that URL
No, but only because the Cache API automatically mirrors every HTTP cache entry
mcqs.explanation: The HTTP cache and the Cache API are independent layers — a fetch() call from worker code still respects standard HTTP caching semantics, and the Cache API is only populated and read when your code explicitly does so.

mcqs.question: Users keep reporting a bug you already fixed and deployed, and refreshing the page doesn't help. What's the most likely service-worker-related cause?
options: The new service worker is stuck in the waiting state because the user's still-open tab is controlled by the old worker, and a plain reload doesn't close it
The user's browser has service workers disabled entirely
The CDN is serving an outdated copy of the service worker script itself
The Cache API has a hard 24-hour expiry that hasn't elapsed yet
mcqs.explanation: This is the 'zombie service worker' pattern — the old worker keeps controlling the page across ordinary reloads because the lifecycle only advances once the tab actually closes, unless skipWaiting/clients.claim force it. There's no built-in 24-hour cache expiry or CDN staleness implied here.
